title: METTL3-mediated m6A modification targets the regulation of PCBP1 expression, thereby modulating GPX4 levels and intracellular Fe2⁺ homeostasis to influence ferroptosis and contribute to juvenile sepsis-associated brain injury.
abstract: Juvenile sepsis-associated brain injury (SABI) lacks effective targeted therapies, and ferroptosis has emerged as a critical pathogenic mechanism. N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) modification is increasingly recognized as a key epitranscriptomic regulator in inflammatory and neurological disorders, yet its role in ferroptosis regulation during SABI remains unexplored. Here, we identify a novel METTL3-PCBP1-ferroptosis axis that drives hippocampal neuronal injury in SABI. Using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)-induced rat SABI model and an in vitro co-culture system of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated microglia with primary hippocampal neurons, we demonstrate that SABI significantly upregulates methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) expression and global m⁶A modification levels in the hippocampus. MeRIP-seq reveals that poly(rC)-binding protein 1 (Pcbp1) mRNA-encoding an iron chaperone that maintains cellular iron homeostasis-exhibits the most pronounced increase in m⁶A modification among cell death-related genes, with site-specific methylation at position 1151 (GGACA motif). This modification recruits the m⁶A reader YTH domain-containing family protein 2 (YTHDF2), promoting Pcbp1 mRNA decay and subsequent PCBP1 protein downregulation. Loss of PCBP1 reduces glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) expression-likely through impaired mRNA binding-and disrupts intracellular Fe2⁺ homeostasis, ultimately triggering ferroptosis characterized by lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial damage. Notably, METTL3 knockdown restores PCBP1 expression, normalizes Fe2⁺ levels, upregulates GPX4, and attenuates ferroptosis and hippocampal injury; however, concurrent PCBP1 knockdown reverses these protective effects. Furthermore, PCBP1 overexpression in SABI rats rescues ferroptosis and neurological deficits. Collectively, our findings establish that METTL3-mediated m⁶A modification of Pcbp1 mRNA exacerbates ferroptosis and SABI pathogenesis, identifying the METTL3/PCBP1 axis as a promising therapeutic target for juvenile SABI.

title: Modeling long-range human nigrostriatal connectivity in vitro reveals striatal target-dependent maturation of dopamine neurons.
abstract: The human nigrostriatal pathway, comprising dopaminergic neurons in the ventral midbrain that project to the dorsolateral striatum, is essential for motor control and selectively vulnerable in Parkinson's disease. How this circuit assembles during human development remains poorly understood, and in vitro models capturing its long-range connectivity and spatial organization have been lacking. Here, we establish a compartmentalized, human stem cell-based model of the nigrostriatal pathway by integrating ventral midbrain and striatal organoids within a custom-engineered microfluidic device that confines cell bodies while guiding axonal growth to recapitulate key aspects of in vivo topography. Functional connectivity was confirmed by retrograde rabies tracing, and optogenetic and pharmacological stimulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis reveals that axonal target engagement with spatially separated striatal neurons promotes maturation of human dopaminergic neurons and activates transcriptional programs associated with neurotransmitter secretion. Our study establishes a biologically relevant in vitro system for investigating how long-range connectivity regulates neuronal assembly in the nigrostriatal circuit and for modelling key pathological features of Parkinson's disease.

title: Freda Newcombe (1925-2001).
Ethics of HIV Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Implementation Research in Inpatient Psychiatry: A Qualitative Study of Patient Perspectives.
abstract: People living with serious mental illness (PLSMI) experience disproportionately high HIV incidence, yet remain underrepresented in HIV prevention research. PLSMI are often excluded from pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) interventions in acute care settings. Inpatient psychiatry units (IPUs) are a promising but unexplored venue for PrEP intervention. However, such research requires designs sensitive to privacy, autonomy, therapeutic misconception, and inflicted insight unique to this population. We conducted semi-structured, qualitative interviews with PLSMI recruited from an academic medical center IPU. Eligible participants were ≥ 18 years old, HIV-negative, met ≥ 1 CDC PrEP-eligibility criterion, and were within 72 h of discharge. Interviews explored five domains: acceptability of IPU-based PrEP research, autonomy and undue influence, dignity and privacy, potential for inflicted insight, and fairness of randomized designs. Transcripts were analyzed thematically. Participants (n = 30; mean age 30.4 years; 80% Black; 72% male) expressed acceptability of PrEP-related research on the IPU, describing participation as informative, engaging, and aligned with their recovery goals. Privacy emerged as a central concern due to the communal IPU environment. Autonomy was consistently emphasized; participants felt more empowered to refuse research than clinical activities, and very few feared consequences for refusal. Views on randomization were mixed: some endorsed its fairness, while others preferred need-based allocation. These findings offer foundational guidance for ethically grounded PrEP research in inpatient psychiatry. PLSMI viewed IPU-based PrEP research as acceptable and potentially beneficial, and identified clear ethical priorities. Future studies should prioritize privacy, reinforce voluntariness, and transparently explain randomization.

title: Effects of motion and white matter hyperintensities on reference region based ¹⁸F-SynVesT-1 PET quantification in Alzheimer's disease and healthy volunteers.
abstract: 18F-SynVesT-1 is a PET tracer targeting synaptic vesicle protein 2A, a surrogate marker of synaptic density. Simplified quantification using pseudo-reference regions such as the centrum semiovale (CSO) or whole cerebellum (CER) has previously been validated in healthy volunteers and Alzheimer's disease. This study assessed how motion correction and white-matter hyperintensities (WMH) affect 18F-SynVesT-1 quantification. We reconstructed 18F-SynVesT-1 images for 40 healthy volunteers and 31 patients with Alzheimer's disease 60-90 minutes post-injection with 3 motion handling methods: no motion correction; 5 minute frame-based post-reconstruction coregistration and averaging, and a high-temporal-resolution data-driven motion correction applied during reconstruction. WMH were segmented from T2-FLAIR images and excluded from the CSO to generate lesion-corrected CSO regions. A region-based voxelwise partial volume correction was applied. SUV and SUVRCSO/CER were compared across motion- and lesion-handling methods and the effects on group differentiation were explored. Data-driven motion correction during reconstruction improved visual image sharpness and increased SUV in high-binding cortical regions (median +0.3-1.0%, p≤0.001) while reducing SUV in the low-binding CSO (median -0.5%, p=0.001). Coregistering and averaging of frames only increased contrast when there was severe motion. The cerebellum was one of the least affected regions by motion correction (median SUV +0.4% with PETDDLM, p<0.001). WMH affected CSO SUV only when ≥25% of the region contained lesions and never affected the cerebellar SUV. SUVRCSO yielded better group differentiation than SUVRCER after accounting for motion and WMH. Individual patients' z-scores differed significantly in both directions depending on the use of SUVRCSO or SUVRCER (e.g. mean absolute difference of 1.00± 0.82 in the precuneus). Data-driven motion correction during reconstruction reduced the impact of head movements and attenuation mismatches, improving image contrast and quantitative accuracy. SUVRCER was less sensitive to motion and WMH than SUVRCSO, indicating greater robustness. When motion and WMH effects were controlled, SUVRCSO provided slightly better group differentiation than SUVRCER. These findings suggest that CSO may be preferred for group comparisons in well-controlled datasets, while the cerebellum represents a more robust reference region in the presence of motion or substantial WMH burden. The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05384353), first posted on 20 May 2022.

title: Metabolic sensor Gpr35 links dietary lipids to itch mediating neural circuits.
abstract: Impact of nutrition on systemic health is well-recognized but the specific sensors that couple western dietary lipid metabolites into the pathological triggers of chronic itch and inflammation remain elusive. Here, we identify a metabolic- to-sensory axis in which 9-keto-12,13-epoxy octadecenoic acid (EKODE), an endogenous dietary linoleic acid derivative acts as a potent ligand for the G protein-coupled receptor 35 (Gpr35) to drive chronic itch, inflammation, and heat hypersensitivity. We demonstrate that Gpr35 is selectively expresses in a distinct population of sensory neurons and genetic ablation of Gpr35 in sensory neurons attenuates EKODE and psoriasis-associated itch and inflammation. Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of Gpr35 significantly attenuates itch in mouse models of psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. We show that Gpr35 signaling engages the itch-specific brain natriuretic peptide, defining a labeled-line pathway that is functionally distinct from classical nociceptive circuits. Collectively, our findings establish Gpr35 as a critical neuro-metabolic sensor in healthy and disease conditions.

title: Developmental pathways to aggression in mental disorders : The child and adolescent perspective of TRR 379.
abstract: Aggression in mental disorders is a clinically and societally highly relevant transdiagnostic phenomenon with heterogeneous developmental trajectories in childhood and adolescence: Aggressive behaviors may occur transiently and decline, but they may also stabilize across adolescence and persist into adulthood. The Collaborative Research Center Transregio 379 "Neuropsychobiology of Aggression: A Transdiagnostic Approach in Mental Disorders" investigates the biological, psychological, and social mechanisms that explain these divergent trajectories. The guiding framework is a developmental model in which aggressive biosignatures emerge from an imbalance between the developing negative valence system and cognitive control. During adolescence, reactivity to social threat, rejection, frustration, and status loss increases, while cognitive control systems continue to mature. Peers, exclusion, victimization, bullying, and puberty-related hormonal changes may shape these maturational processes. This article describes the child and adolescent developmental projects of TRR 379 and the longitudinal cohort. Understanding transdiagnostic biosignatures opens new opportunities for preventive and mechanism-based therapeutic interventions during critical windows of developmental plasticity.

title: Sex- and frequency-dependent acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects of smoked cannabis: a randomized controlled trial.
journal: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
abstract: Cannabis use is rising among women. Studies suggest females are more sensitive to the intoxicating and misuse-related effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). While preclinical studies point to sex-specific development of tolerance, this has not been translated to humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 44 participants (22 F) smoked three cannabis strengths (0% [~0 mg] THC, 4% [~20 mg] THC, 10% [~60 mg] THC), provided blood for plasma analysis, and completed subjective mood and drug effects assessments and a self-administration task. Outcomes were analyzed by cannabis strength, sex, and use frequency ( > 4 vs. ≤4 days/week; balanced across sex). Relative to placebo, active cannabis strengths increased subjective effects and plasma THC and metabolites (ps < 0.05). Exploratory follow-up of interactions (cannabis strength*frequency p < 0.10) showed the frequent-use group exhibiting significant increases from placebo in misuse-related ratings ("Like", "Take again") and self-administering more cannabis than the occasional-use group (ps < 0.05), and this was not modified by sex. Ratings of "High", Sedation/impairment, Dysphoric arousal, and "Bad effect" were higher at active strengths for occasional-use males relative to sex- and/or frequency-matched counterparts (ps < 0.05; via exploratory follow-up for "High" and Sedation/impairment). THC and metabolites tended to be highest in frequent-use males. These findings contrast with previous evidence of greater cannabis sensitivity among females and point toward future investigation into sex-dependent exposure thresholds for tolerance development/escalation. Sex and frequency of use are both implicated in cannabis use disorder risk, and consideration of their interaction is critical in characterizing the acute effects of, and tolerance to, cannabis.

title: Glymphatic Dysfunction as a Multisystem Pathway Linking Systemic Health Conditions to Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms, Risk Factors, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: The glymphatic system is a glia-associated perivascular pathway involved in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-interstitial fluid (ISF) exchange and the transport and clearance of neurotoxic metabolites, including amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau, from the central nervous system. Growing evidence suggests that alterations in glymphatic and perivascular clearance are associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and may contribute to the accumulation of neurotoxic proteins and neurodegeneration. This review examines the role of the glymphatic system in AD and explores how aging, sleep disturbances, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, high-fat diet, diabetes, and gut microbiome dysbiosis impair glymphatic transport. A recurring mechanism across experimental models is the loss of perivascular AQP4 polarization, while vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory conditions may converge on related perivascular and neurovascular processes that impair CSF-ISF exchange and solute handling. Neuroimaging studies using markers such as DTI-ALPS, perivascular space burden, and free-water measurements provide evidence of alterations in glymphatic-related and perivascular processes in AD and demonstrate associations with amyloid deposition, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline. Furthermore, glymphatic dysfunction may interact with neuroinflammation and tau pathology, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that accelerates disease progression. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including continuous theta-burst stimulation, positive airway pressure therapy for obstructive sleep apnea, pharmacological enhancement of AQP4 function, and nutritional interventions, have shown potential in experimental and early translational studies to influence glymphatic-related processes and may mitigate AD-related pathology. Collectively, current findings suggest that glymphatic and perivascular clearance pathways may represent an important link between systemic health conditions and AD. Because related pathways are implicated across multiple systemic conditions, interventions targeting glymphatic and perivascular dysfunction may have broader relevance to brain health, but their clinical effects remain to be established.

title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut-brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. Moreover, we synthesize current evidence demonstrating that microbiota-dependent tryptophan metabolism exhibits distinct profiles across clinical, demographic, immunometabolic, trauma-related, and genetically defined depressive phenotypes, thereby establishing its role as a unifying biological framework underlying depressive heterogeneity. We further provide a critical appraisal of emerging therapeutic strategies targeting microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism, including pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions. Future investigations should integrate multi-omics approaches, longitudinal study designs, and mechanistic validation with artificial intelligence to elucidate causal relationships between microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism and depressive heterogeneity, ultimately facilitating biomarker discovery and the development of precision therapeutics.

title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM. Partial genetic correlations revealed that ALCP and PTSD were associated with each other (rG = 0.39, p = 4.38 × 10-60) and with other psychiatric problems, medical conditions, and pain, while ALCC was only weakly correlated with PTSD (rG = -0.08, p = 2.03 × 10-4) and uncorrelated with most traits after accounting for its genetic overlap with ALCP and PTSD. We examined associations between GenomicSEM-derived polygenic scores (PGS) and their corresponding phenotypes in participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA). PGS for ALCC were unrelated to PTSD diagnosis and PGS for PTSD were unrelated to drinks in a typical week. PTSD is more strongly related to alcohol problems, and much of the overlap in PTSD and consumption is accounted for by its overlap with alcohol problems. These results help demonstrate the complex partial overlaps of PTSD, AUD, and alcohol consumption.

title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential.
abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

title: A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability.
abstract: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.

title: Invisible shield: sprayable supramolecular antimicrobial microscale films for preventing wound and medical device infections.
abstract: Wound and device-associated infections remain difficult to eradicate because biofilms limit host immunity and antibiotic efficacy, promoting chronicity and resistance. Here, we present a portable, low-cost dual-syringe spray that deposits a thin, self-assembling antimicrobial film directly on wounds and implant surfaces. The device co-delivers oppositely charged hyaluronic acid (HA) and polyarginine (PAR30), a cationic antimicrobial peptide, which rapidly assembles into a conformal micrometric polyelectrolyte complex at the tissue-material interface. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed positional heterogeneity within the PAR30/HA complex and identified an N-terminal arginine as a dominant interaction hotspot. The resulting coating adheres to diverse substrates, kills bacteria on contact, prevents biofilm formation, and sustains antimicrobial efficacy. The treatment exhibited broad-spectrum in vitro activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli. In murine wound infection models, the spray coating significantly reduced MRSA bacterial burden. The formulation was biocompatible, did not increase cutaneous inflammation or IL6 levels in vivo, and reduced post-surgical pain and motor deficits in a mouse incision model. Developed within a safe-and-sustainable-by-design framework, this technology offers a scalable, antibiotic-free strategy for wound-care and medical-device infection prevention.

title: TNF signaling at the brain-heart interface: neurovascular injury and cardiovascular vulnerability in epilepsy.
abstract: Epilepsy is increasingly viewed as a systemic disorder in which recurrent seizures intersect with vascular, autonomic, respiratory, and cardiac processes to influence cardiovascular vulnerability. Seizure-related neuroinflammation involves multiple interacting mediator pathways, including HMGB1/TLR4-RAGE signaling, inflammasome/IL-1β activation, IL-6/IL-6R-gp130 signaling, albumin/TGF-β signaling following blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)/TNF receptor (TNFR) signaling. Within this inflammatory network, TNF/TNFR signaling represents a mechanistically distinct and translationally relevant framework for examining how immune activation intersects with endothelial-barrier dysfunction, neurovascular unit injury, autonomic disturbance, inflammatory communication across neural and cardiovascular compartments, and cardiac vulnerability. This review integrates direct evidence from epilepsy studies with mechanistic insights from related experimental studies of BBB injury, myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, cardioprotection, and brain-heart communication. TNF biology is determined by ligand form, receptor subtype, cellular compartment, and disease context. Soluble TNF preferentially engages TNFR1-associated inflammatory and injury-amplifying pathways, whereas transmembrane TNF/TNFR2 signaling may support regulatory or reparative responses in selected settings. In epilepsy, seizure-associated inflammation, BBB dysfunction, glial activation, and autonomic imbalance may interact to increase susceptibility to arrhythmogenic stress, myocardial injury, adverse cardiac remodeling, and cardiorespiratory instability relevant to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). However, epilepsy-specific evidence directly linking TNF/TNFR signaling to cardiovascular outcomes remains limited, and many mechanistic connections currently rely on converging evidence from neurovascular and cardiovascular research. Future studies should integrate compartment-resolved inflammatory profiling with autonomic, respiratory, electrocardiographic, and cardiac phenotyping to distinguish inflammatory signatures of disease severity from modifiable contributors to cardiovascular risk. Such approaches may enable phenotype-specific strategies to better understand and ultimately mitigate the brain-heart consequences of epilepsy.

title: Author Correction: Integrating central nervous system metagenomics and host response for diagnosis of tuberculosis meningitis and its mimics.
Amygdala beta bursts modulate hippocampal neuronal dynamics during human emotional processing.
abstract: The amygdala and hippocampus are key structures in emotional processing, yet the transient neural dynamics coordinating their interaction remain poorly understood. We simultaneously recorded single-neuron activity and local field potentials from these regions in epilepsy patients performing an emotional image-rating task. Neurons in both regions exhibited firing rate changes predictive of subjective emotional valence. While conventional spectral analysis revealed no valence-specific patterns, beta bursts (13-30 Hz)-transient, high-power events-were selectively modified by task features. In both regions, beta bursts were associated with increased gamma amplitude and enhanced phase coherence, with beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling capturing emotion-related dynamics. Critically, amygdala beta bursts were associated with valence-dependent, bidirectional modulation of hippocampal interneuron firing - decreased during very unpleasant/highest arousal processing and increased during high-arousal very pleasant processing - while putative pyramidal-cell firing did not change significantly. Hippocampal bursts showed no reciprocal influence. These findings suggest that beta bursts may represent a temporally precise neural correlate of emotional appraisal and a potential target for neuromodulation in mood disorders.

title: Chlorophyll as a sustainable crosslinking strategy for engineering highly compressible hydrogels.
abstract: Hydrogels are promising candidates for tissue repair. Non-invasive delivery of hydrogel patches involving high strains and deformations requires mechanical robustness and complex material design. Here we show chlorophyll, a sustainable plant-derived small molecule, functions as a universal physical crosslinker to significantly enhance hydrogels' compressibility and resilience. Chlorophylls self-assemble in aqueous pre-polymer solution via hydrophobic interactions, leading to the nano-aggregations, acting as physical crosslinkers and anchoring points within hydrogels' matrix. Additionally, the solvent exchange (SE) process promotes macroporous structure formation for high compressibility and resilience. With chlorophyll, the maximum compressive strains of gelatin methacrylate (GC) hydrogels increased from ~43% to ≥90%, allowing injection under 90.4% deformation while preserving structural integrity. This strategy enabled the fabrication of a single 36-mm diameter injectable conductive polypyrrole-deposited GC (GCP) cardiac patch for myocardial repair in minipigs. Moreover, chlorophyll functions as an intrinsic antioxidant reservoir, and improved ejection fraction (EF) by 11 % in porcine infarcted hearts.

title: Clock neurons modulate seizure timing through a diurnal switch.
abstract: People with epilepsy experience daily oscillations in seizure risk. Using a video-tracking model to automate detection, we explored mechanisms underlying spontaneous seizures in Drosophila and find that flies, like people, exhibit daily oscillations in seizure risk. These rhythms are absent in flies lacking a molecular circadian clock and are independent of sleep. Thermogenetic screening and cell-specific clock perturbations reveal that the ventrolateral neurons, including "morning cells", and dorsolateral neurons, comprising the "evening cells", modulate diurnal oscillations in seizure risk. Pigment-dispersing factor and short neuropeptide F from morning cells increase seizure risk during the day. During this time, morning cell activity increases whole-brain activity. At night, morning cells switch to glycine signaling likely acting on evening cells to decrease seizure risk. Optogenetic inhibition of clock neurons suppresses seizure risk. Our findings reveal an unexpected role for brain clock neurons in modulating daily seizure risk.

title: Zona incerta somatostatin+ neurons modulate seizure progression through hypothalamic circuits.
abstract: GABAergic neurons critically regulate epileptic seizures, yet circuit mechanisms mediated by subtype-specific GABAergic neurons in the zona incerta (ZI) remain unclear. Here we reveal the essential role of ZI somatostatin+ GABAergic neurons in seizure modulation in the mouse hippocampal kindling model. In vivo Ca2+ fiber photometry and optogenetics show that ZI GABAergic neurons are gradually activated during seizure progression. Opto-activation inhibits seizure progression, especially the spread of generalized seizures at the later phase, whereas opto-inhibition accelerates it. Although both somatostatin+ and parvalbumin+ neurons are dynamically recruited during seizure progression, only somatostatin+ neurons exert bidirectional seizure modulation. Circuitry mapping and functional modulation demonstrate that ZI somatostatin+ neurons projecting to the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) glutamatergic neurons suppress the spread of generalized seizures by inhibiting the excitability of VMH-related downstream seizure-spread regions. These findings uncover a cell-type-specific circuit mechanism for seizure regulation by ZI somatostatin+ neurons, highlighting these neurons as a potential therapeutic target for epilepsy.

title: Different concentrations of atropine in children with high myopia: a 2-year multicenter double-blind, randomized controlled trial.
abstract: High myopia in children risks irreversible visual impairment, yet optimal interventions remain debated. This multicenter double-blind, randomized-controlled trial aims to evaluate the effect and safety of different atropine eyedrops for myopia control in children with high myopia, conducted in Shanghai Eye Diseases Prevention and Treatment Center, Shanghai General Hospital and Shanghai Ninth People's Hospital. Recruitment started on July 4th, 2021 and final follow-up was August, 21st, 2024. 219 children aged 6-12 years with myopia of at least -5.0 diopter (D) were recruited and randomly assigned to use either 0.01%(N = 76), 0.04%(N = 72), or 0.10%(N = 71) atropine eyedrops once nightly for both eyes over 24 months, and 182 participants completed trial; 219 (76:72:71) randomized cases were analyzed. Main outcome was cycloplegic spherical equivalent (SE) change from baseline over 24 months. After 24 months, mean SE progression was -0.92 D, -0.78 D and -0.56 D for 0.01%, 0.04% and 0.10% atropine, respectively. The 0.10% atropine significantly reduced myopia progression by 0.35 D (95%CI: 0.12 D, 0.58 D) versus 0.01%, while 0.04% atropine did not show significant difference; however, at 12 months, both higher concentrations demonstrated significantly greater reductions (0.16 D and 0.30 D for 0.04% and 0.10%, respectively). Photophobia was the most common adverse event, reported by 9.0%, 10.6% and 18.8% in 0.01%, 0.04% and 0.10% atropine respectively in 12 months and 7.8%, 8.1% and 21.1% in 24 months. These results demonstrated that in children aged 6-12 years with high myopia, nightly use of 0.10% atropine for 24 months effectively and safely attenuated myopia progression. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04699357.

title: Temporal elements of speech in mania.
abstract: Computational analysis of speech enables precise, objective measurements of a behavioral signal closely linked to manic episodes. In a prospective cohort study conducted in Rochester, MN (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05956340), eighteen English-speaking adults voluntarily hospitalized for a manic episode of Bipolar I Disorder between August 2023 and September 2024 were enrolled. Participants completed semi-structured research interviews during both acute episodes and remission, with manic symptom severity assessed at each session using the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS). Across 57 recorded interviews, temporal prosodic features were extracted using a novel end-to-end computational pipeline. After adjusting for individual differences and moderating effects, participant articulation rate (β = 0.24, p = 0.0038), speech rate variability (β = 0.23, p = 0.0041), floor transfer offset (β = -0.31, p = 0.007), and speaking duration (β = 0.54, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with manic symptom severity. These exploratory findings were largely independent of medication effects, as well as the presence of psychotic or mixed symptoms. These temporal elements classified manic (CV AUC = 0.85) and remission (CV AUC = 0.83) status, highlighting their potential as monitoring biomarkers for manic episodes.

title: Emotional intensity and visual imagery in trauma nightmares map to posterior hippocampus connectivity.
abstract: Distressing dreams or nightmares about a traumatic experience are common among trauma-exposed individuals and contribute to the maintenance of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms. Like other intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, trauma-related nightmares are characterized by vivid sensory details and heightened emotional intensity. However, little is known about their underlying neurobiology, and whether it overlaps with that of diurnal reexperiencing symptoms. Therefore, this study aimed to elucidate neurobiological correlates of the phenomenology of trauma-related nightmares. Sixty-six trauma-exposed adults (54 female) completed daily ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) of the phenomenological properties of their trauma-related nightmares for two weeks, as well as resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Pearson correlations examined associations between nightmare properties and functional connectivity within two a priori circuits previously implicated in trauma-related intrusions and episodic memory: 1) an affective circuit between the anterior hippocampus (aHPC) and amygdala (Amyg), and 2) a sensory circuit between the posterior hippocampus (pHPC) and visual cortex (VC). There were no significant associations between nightmare properties and aHPC-Amyg connectivity. In contrast, stronger pHPC-VC connectivity was associated with greater visual detail and emotional intensity of nightmares. These findings align with the established roles of the pHPC and VC in the detailed experience of episodic memory and suggest a novel role for these regions in the affective features of trauma nightmares. Overall, these findings provide support for overlapping neural correlates of the properties of trauma nightmares and diurnal reexperiencing symptoms. They offer additional evidence for a pHPC-VC circuit as a promising neurotherapeutic target for trauma reexperiencing symptoms.

title: Hippocampal subregion volume alterations at baseline and following antidepressant treatment in youth at high risk for bipolar disorder.
abstract: Understanding hippocampal neurostructural alterations at baseline and following antidepressant treatment in high-risk youth, particularly within distinct subregions, is critical for elucidating bipolar disorder (BD) pathophysiology and treatment planning. In this prospective randomized clinical trial, 105 high-risk youth with a first-degree BD-I relative(s) and moderate to severe depression and/or anxiety disorder, along with 51 healthy controls (HCs), were recruited. All participants underwent baseline structural MRI and clinical evaluations for depression, anxiety, and adverse events. High-risk youth were then randomized to receive psychotherapy and with either escitalopram or placebo. After 4 weeks of treatment, high-risk youth underwent repeated structural MRI and clinical assessments. These clinical assessments continued biweekly over the remaining 12 weeks of treatment (up to week 16). Volumetric measurements of hippocampal subregions were analyzed at baseline and 4 weeks. Compared to HCs, high-risk youth had significant baseline volume increases in the right cornu ammonis (CA)3, bilateral CA4, bilateral granule cell and molecular layers of the dentate gyrus (GC-ML-DG), and bilateral molecular layer, but reduced volumes in the bilateral fimbria and left parasubiculum. Volume reduction in the left hippocampal tail after 4 weeks of escitalopram treatment was associated with improvements in disinhibition and impulsivity symptoms from baseline to 4 weeks, and this association remained significant from baseline to 16 weeks. CA3-4 and GC-ML-DG enlargement may reflect adaptive changes, while fimbria and parasubiculum atrophy indicate vulnerabilities in BD-risk youth. Escitalopram-related volume reduction in the left hippocampal tail may reflect neural plasticity associated with emotional symptom improvement in BD high-risk youth. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION INFORMATION: Mechanism of Antidepressant-Related Dysfunctional Arousal in High-Risk Youth; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ ; NCT02553161.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in microbiota-gut-brain axis research: Implications for Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiota (GM) are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA), influencing neuroinflammation, amyloid-β deposition, and tau aggregation. The inherent complexity of microbiota data necessitates artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. In this narrative review, we examined AI applications in AD-related GM research, including metataxonomic and metagenomic approaches. AI methods facilitate microbial signature identification and enterotype characterization associated with AD progression, enable multi-omics integration clarifying molecular pathways linking GM dysbiosis to neurodegeneration, support predictive modeling for early AD detection, and inform personalized MGBA-targeted interventions. Employed techniques include classical ML (e.g., random forests) for taxonomic classification, deep learning (e.g., neural networks) for complex pattern recognition, and explainable AI for identifying key bacterial taxa and metabolic functions. Significant challenges persist regarding methodological standardization, larger longitudinal cohorts, and ethical considerations in clinical applications. Future priorities include developing interpretable models, integrating longitudinal multi-omics data to establish causality, and validating AI-derived insights for precision AD prevention and treatment. AI uniquely enables high-dimensional, non-linear analyses that advance understanding of microbiome-brain interactions, though clinical translation requires rigorous validation and interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: Cross-species mapping of acute psychedelic-responsive genes links HTR2A cortical expression, cell-type enrichment, and human cortical expression modules.
abstract: Psychedelic drugs exert rapid and profound effects on human consciousness [1-7] and are increasingly being investigated for their therapeutic potential [8-14]. Yet the transcriptional programs through which they may reshape brain function and structure remain incompletely understood, in part because the available evidence is heterogeneous and largely preclinical [15, 16]. In a structured scoping review of transcriptomic studies in animal models and neural cell cultures, we identified genes reported in the source literature to change within 3 h of classical psychedelic administration and intersected them with the Allen Human Brain Atlas to define an acute expression set. This retained set showed cortex-centered enrichment, a marker-based deep-layer projection-neuron component, and ontology enrichment for neuron projection and related synaptic terms. A smaller subset overlapped with human accelerated region-associated genes and showed greater-than-random spatial alignment with a human cortical-expansion map. The retained cortical-expression maps showed serotonergic spatial alignment in the human cortex, most prominently with HTR2A expression. Clustering identified three cortical spatial-expression modules, including an association/limbic-weighted module enriched for plasticity and synaptic-organization terms. Together, these findings provide a human cortical framework linking acute psychedelic-responsive transcription to cortical cell-type enrichment, HTR2A spatial expression, cortical spatial-expression modules, and cortical-expansion, while leaving receptor-specific, causal, translational, and cell-type-resolved mechanisms for future work.

title: Gut microbiota-derived TNF-α triggers dopaminergic neuron ferroptosis via TNFR1-NF-κB-ATF4 axis in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, with the causal link between gut microbiota dysbiosis and central neurodegeneration unclarified. This study aimed to unravel this complex interplay by integrating Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis, animal models, cellular experiments, and transcriptomic profiling. MR analysis identified Clostridium sensu stricto 1 and Candidatus Soleaferrea as novel genetic risk factors for PD, providing causal evidence for gut microbiota-driven PD pathogenesis. Using a chronic MPTP-induced PD mouse model, we confirmed that gut microbiota dysbiosis is accompanied by elevated tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) in the intestine, plasma, and midbrain, along with dopaminergic neuron loss and motor deficits. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy mice reversed these phenotypes, restoring gut homeostasis, reducing TNF-α levels, and preserving dopaminergic neurons. Transcriptomic analysis of mouse midbrain and human PD substantia nigra (GEO datasets) revealed ferroptosis as a key enriched pathway, with activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) significantly upregulated in both PD models and patients. Mechanistically, TNF-α induced ATF4 overexpression in a concentration- and time-dependent manner, triggering dopaminergic neuron ferroptosis. This effect was mediated by TNF-α binding to TNFR1 (not TNFR2), activating the NF-κB pathway, and subsequently upregulating ATF4. Knockdown of ATF4 or inhibition of NF-κB reversed TNF-α-induced ferroptosis, as evidenced by restored glutathione (GSH) levels, reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation, and improved cell viability. Our findings establish a novel gut-brain axis-mediated pathogenic pathway: gut microbiota dysbiosis drives TNF-α-TNFR1-NF-κB-ATF4 signaling, leading to dopaminergic neuron ferroptosis and PD progression. This study bridges the gap between peripheral microbial dysbiosis and central neurodegeneration, identifies potential therapeutic targets, and highlights FMT as a promising intervention for PD.

title: Functional connectivity of anterior cingulate cortex subregions in suicidal ideation in major depression: circuit mechanisms, exploratory classification, and treatment-related changes.
abstract: Suicidal ideation (SI) is a critical challenge in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its precise neural circuitry remains elusive. Although anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is implicated, its subregional roles remain poorly understood. This study aimed to delineate SI-specific neural circuitry by examining whole-brain functional connectivity (FC) of ACC subregions: subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), and dorsal ACC (dACC). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 237 MDD patients (109 with SI [MDD-SI], 128 without SI [MDD-NSI]) and 152 healthy controls (HCs) at baseline. Group assignment relied on lifetime SI (trait-like SI) from the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, with current SI (state-like SI) measured by the suicide item of 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Of these, 129 MDD patients underwent 8-week follow-up scanning after treatment. Cross-sectional analysis identified two SI-specific FC alterations: left pgACC-right precuneus and left dACC-left fusiform connectivity. These FCs were enhanced in MDD-SI compared to MDD-NSI, showed no differences between MDD-NSI and HCs, and correlated with trait-like SI severity. An exploratory model incorporating these FCs and clinical covariates achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.723 for trait-like SI identification. Longitudinally, the baseline elevation in left pgACC-right precuneus FC normalized after treatment specifically in MDD-SI, and this reduction paralleled the decrease in state-like SI severity. Our findings clarify ACC subregion-specific SI mechanisms, provide an exploratory evaluation of trait-like SI identification and identify a potential state-like SI therapeutic circuit. Collectively, this work translates vague ACC abnormality into localizable circuits, advancing precision neuroscience for MDD-SI.

title: Machine Learning in the Differential Diagnosis of Bipolar and Borderline Personality Disorders: A Scoping Review.
journal: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie
abstract: BackgroundBipolar disorder (BD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) are associated with substantial morbidity and can be difficult to distinguish when symptoms are assessed cross-sectionally. This scoping review examines machine learning (ML) and related predictive approaches designed to differentiate the two conditions.MethodsWe searched Ovid MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and selected computer science conference proceedings through July 2, 2026. Full-text peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers were eligible when they used a data-driven computational or statistical prediction approach to distinguish, classify, or characterize BD and BPD. Of 2,594 records identified, 2,523 unique records were screened, and 24 full texts were assessed. Screening followed the Population, Concept, Context framework, Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses extension for scoping reviews.ResultsNine reports met the inclusion criteria. Seven participant-based reports contributed an aggregate of 986 report-level participants, although two reports used overlapping cohorts; one conference paper used synthetic data, and one study analyzed 149,798 Reddit posts. Studies including clinical samples reported BD versus BPD discrimination AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) values of 0.67 to 0.91 and accuracies ranging from 61.7% to 90%. These estimates were not directly comparable and were derived from small, often imbalanced samples using heterogeneous internal validation. No model was externally validated in an independent clinical cohort.ConclusionThe evidence remains preliminary and does not support clinical deployment. Reported performance is constrained by small samples, class imbalance, uncertain ground-truth labels, spectrum bias, and reliance on pre-existing diagnoses. Prospective studies in consecutive at-risk cohorts, with transparent reporting and independent external validation, are required.

title: Improving the Diagnostic Accuracy of Plasma Alzheimer's Disease Biomarkers With Objective and Subjective Cognitive Screening.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
abstract: Blood-based biomarkers are increasingly used to identify Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and may play an important role in early disease screening and participant selection for clinical trials. However, their performance across stages of cognitive impairment remains unclear. This study examined whether plasma biomarkers differ in their ability to predict amyloid pathology by performance on cognitive screening measures. Participants were older adults from the community-based Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project (N = 154; mean age = 72 ± 6 years; 37% MCI). Plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau)231 and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured using Quanterix Simoa technology. Amyloid positivity was defined by cerebrospinal fluid β-amyloid 42/40 ratio < 0.072. Objective cognitive impairment was defined as ≤ 26 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment; cognitive complaints were assessed by a single-item self-report. Logistic regression and stratified ROC analyses evaluated associations between biomarkers and amyloid status, with area under the ROC curve (AUC) values compared using DeLong's test. Forty-seven percent of participants were amyloid positive. Higher plasma p-tau231 was associated with increased odds of amyloid positivity (OR = 1.18, p < 0.001; AUC = 0.73). Discriminative accuracy was significantly higher among individuals without subjective cognitive concerns (AUC = 0.85) than among those individuals with concerns (AUC = 0.67; p = 0.02). Plasma GFAP was also associated with amyloid positivity (OR = 1.01, p < 0.001; AUC = 0.75) and showed greater accuracy among participants with objective cognitive impairment (AUC = 0.82) compared to unimpaired individuals (AUC = 0.63; p = 0.03). Plasma p-tau231 and GFAP were associated with amyloid pathology, but their diagnostic accuracy varied by cognitive screening results, highlighting the value of integrating brief cognitive assessments when interpreting blood-based biomarkers.

title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self-environment interaction 'here and now'.
abstract: The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body-object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body-object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

title: SpaCon: scalable spatial transcriptomic and connectomic integration.
Distinct Associations of Age and CYP2D6 Genotype With Parent Venlafaxine Exposure and O-Demethylation in Japanese Psychiatric Patients.
abstract: Venlafaxine (VEN) is converted to O-desmethylvenlafaxine (ODV) mainly through CYP2D6-mediated O-demethylation. However, age-related clinical factors may also influence VEN exposure in routine practice. We examined whether age and CYP2D6 genotype show different associations with parent-drug exposure and metabolic conversion. This retrospective therapeutic drug monitoring analysis included 78 Japanese psychiatric patients with available plasma VEN and ODV concentrations and CYP2D6 genotype data. Two prespecified outcomes were analyzed without body-weight correction: VEN concentration divided by daily dose (VEN/dose) and the ODV/VEN ratio. CYP2D6*10 and *5 were coded as reduced- and no-function alleles, respectively. Log-transformed outcomes were analyzed using regression models including age and CYP2D6 reduced/no-function allele count. Nineteen patients (24.4%) were aged 65 years or older. Age was correlated with VEN/dose (Spearman rho = 0.295, p = 0.0086), and older patients had higher VEN/dose than younger patients (median, 0.522 vs. 0.192 [ng/mL]/[mg/day], p = 0.0127). In regression analysis, the incremental R2 for age was numerically larger than that for CYP2D6 allele count for VEN/dose (incremental R2, 0.058 vs. 0.026). Conversely, the ODV/VEN ratio was strongly associated with CYP2D6 allele count (standardized beta = -0.391, p < 0.001; incremental R2 = 0.145) but not with age. Age-by-genotype interactions were not significant for either outcome. Age appeared to be more closely related to dose-corrected parent VEN exposure, whereas CYP2D6 genotype predominantly determined the ODV/VEN metabolic ratio. The relative contribution of age should be interpreted descriptively because no formal comparison of effect sizes was performed. Separating exposure and metabolic-ratio outcomes may clarify how geriatric and pharmacogenetic factors contribute to VEN disposition.

title: Can Spleen T1 Mapping Be Used as a Marker of Adenosine Response in Cardiac MRI?
abstract: Splenic switch-off, defined as the visible reduction in splenic perfusion during adenosine stress, can be used as a marker of adequate adenosine response in cardiac stress MRI studies, which can be assessed after the study. Moreover, there is some evidence regarding the use of T1 mapping for the evaluation of splenic switch-off during the study. The aim of this work is to further investigate splenic T1 mapping as a method for quantitatively assessing splenic switch-off, given the limited existing data. Patients with suspected coronary artery disease were scanned at 1.5 T with the routine clinical protocol for stress perfusion cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), including a T1 mapping sequence at rest and during adenosine stress. Visual assessment of first-pass images was used as the reference standard for detecting splenic switch-off. Semi-quantitative analysis of splenic perfusion was performed based on the signal intensity curves and signal changes (ΔSI) were calculated. T1 maps were used to obtain T1 value changes in the spleen from rest to stress (ΔT1spleen). Statistical analysis was assessed using an align rank transform followed by a mixed analysis of variance, with Bonferroni corrected post hoc tests. A total of 74.5% (n = 35/47) of analyzed patients experienced splenic switch-off according to the visual assessment. Statistically significant differences were found in splenic T1 between rest and stress only in the switch-off group (p < 0.001), with lower T1 values during stress. There was significant positive weak correlation (ρs = 0.37, p = 0.01) between splenic ΔT1 and ΔSI based on first-pass. ROC curves demonstrated that ΔT1spleen classified the failed switch-off and positive switch-off groups with a specificity of 75% and a sensitivity of 80% (AUC: 81.2%, 95% CI: 66.7%-95.8%). This work indicates that the splenic T1 value change has the potential to identify splenic switch-off during adenosine stress CMR in a clinical population.

title: Nobel 2026: Optogenetics - how we can control the nerve cells of others!
Circadian clock adjusted classes improve sleep, circadian health, and academic performance in medical freshmen.
abstract: University students often experience circadian misalignment with academic schedules, which may impair performance. This study evaluated whether a later-start schedule improves academic outcomes and circadian rhythms in first-year medical students. Incoming students (n = 220) completed the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire; those with high social jetlag (SJL >120 min, n = 71) were randomized into either a later-start schedule (LS; classes ≥10:00 a.m., n = 30) or a standard early-start schedule (ES; 8:00 a.m., n = 41). Actigraphy data were collected from 112 students prior to examinations. Based on the objective temperature circadian phase (TCP) with a median acrophase split at 3:59 a.m. ES participants were categorized asearly (ETCP-ES, n = 41) or late (LTCP-ES, n = 41). All LS participants exhibited a TCP later than 3:59 a.m. and remained LTCP-LS group (n = 30). Associations between scheduling, circadian metrics, and exam scores were analyzed using regression and sex-adjusted ANCOVA. TCP predicted exam scores overall (β = -0.217, p = 0.021), most evidently within ES (β = -0.291, p = 0.008). LTCP-ES students scored lower than ETCP-ES students (p = 0.025). LTCP-LS students performed similarly to ETCP-ES students and showed greater circadian robustness, including higher rest-activity stability (p = 0.031), greater blue-light stability (p = 0.029), and longer sleep duration (p = 0.013).

title: Novel Radiotracers in PET Imaging.
abstract: This article reviews emerging PET radiopharmaceuticals in late preclinical and early clinical development. The discussed tracers have broad applications for disease staging, theranostic patient selection, and treatment monitoring. For oncology, tracers targeting fibroblast activation protein, prostate-specific membrane antigen, delta-like ligand 3, trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2, claudin 18.2, and amino-acid transporters are highlighted alongside immune-targeted tracers imaging cluster of differentiation proteins, the programmed death-1 receptor and ligand, granzyme B, and macrophages. In neurology, tracers targeting amyloid-beta, tau, translocator protein, and synaptic vesicle protein 2A are discussed. Highlighted cardiology tracers focus on imaging of myocardial perfusion, amyloidosis, and vascular inflammation.

title: Retinal Neurovascular Structure in Colombian Patients With Early-Course Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders.
abstract: Previous studies have suggested that the neurovascular structure of the retina is affected in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD). However, no research has investigated this in Colombian patients. This cross-sectional study explores whether individuals diagnosed with early-course SSD exhibit distinct retinal structure and microvasculature compared to healthy controls (HCs) and whether these differences correlate with clinical, course-related, and cognitive variables. Patients diagnosed with schizophrenia (n=20) or schizoaffective disorder (n=2) and age/gender-matched HCs (n=21) were included. Retinal structure was assessed using Optical Coherence Tomography - Angiography. Statistical analyses included general linear models adjusted for covariates such as age, gender, spherical equivalent, and smoking status. Associations between retinal measures and clinical or cognitive variables were explored using linear regression and correlation analyses. Retinal measures were generally lower in patients than in HCs, with statistically significant differences observed only in the right eye's inferior and average macular deep vessel density (VD). Symptom severity was inversely correlated with Ganglion Cell Complex thickness and macular/papillary VD. The premorbid adjustment was associated with vascular measures but not neural tissue measures, while the duration of untreated psychosis was unrelated to any retinal measures. Longer time since the last hospitalization and better cognitive performance were linked to a thicker retinal structure. Retina could provide valuable and rapid information in real-world settings about brain health in SSD, so longitudinal studies on neurovascular retinal structure, including metabolic, inflammatory, and neuroimaging variables, in prodromal and early-course SSD are needed.

title: Why dentists should return to the anatomy laboratory.
abstract: Anatomy has traditionally been taught as a foundational subject completed before clinical dental training, with limited opportunities for structured anatomical education after graduation. However, advances in implant dentistry, periodontal and regenerative surgery, injectable therapies, imaging, and orofacial pain management increasingly require detailed and clinically contextualized anatomical knowledge. This Perspective argues that anatomy should be regarded as a lifelong component of dental education rather than a preclinical prerequisite. Clinical experience generates anatomical questions that students may not yet recognize, allowing practicing dentists to reinterpret anatomy through the lens of patient care. At the same time, contemporary anatomical research continues to identify clinically relevant variations, tissue relationships, and structural continuities, demonstrating that anatomy remains an active clinical science. Continuing professional development should therefore incorporate clinically oriented anatomy education, particularly cadaveric dissection, which enables direct appreciation of anatomical variability, tissue planes, three-dimensional relationships, and operative perspectives. The goal is not simply to teach dentists more anatomy, but to help them ask better anatomical questions throughout their careers. Integrating anatomy into continuing education may improve clinical decision-making, prevent avoidable complications, enhance patient outcomes, and reduce associated medicolegal risk.

title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8-13 Hz) and beta (14-30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels.Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.

title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior.Significance Statement The habenula - an epithalamic brain region - plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

title: PTPRO restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors through TrkB dephosphorylation.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration.Significance Statement How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.

title: Hexagonal modulation of theta rhythmic attentional sampling of visual space.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition.Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

title: Area MT carries acceleration information in a quickly and directly decodable representation.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: We sought to better understand the neural representation of visual motion acceleration. A straightforward estimation of acceleration would involve calculating the rate of change of velocity, which itself would be calculated from change in position over time. As it is well-established that neurons in area MT encode velocity, the brain could thus indirectly estimate acceleration by calculating the change in MT's velocity representations. An alternative mechanism, however, could operate more rapidly and directly. In this case, the brain could exploit interactions between MT's standard motion encoding and idiosyncratic temporal dynamics of neural responses. Such direct decoding would thus exploit nonlinearities usually ignored in studies of MT coding. We tested between these two theories by measuring from ensembles of MT neurons while two male awake fixating macaques viewed linearly accelerating motion stimuli. Direct decoding of acceleration from MT was possible on faster time scales, and could be done with higher fidelity, than indirect decoding. Distinct motion acceleration information could thus be efficiently read out from rich and heterogeneous MT ensemble responses, regardless of the mechanisms that give rise to various forms of motion tuning that it exhibits. A similar analysis of activity in the medial superior temporal area (MST) did not suggest that this later stage of motion processing has a more refined acceleration representation. Together, these results suggest that the brain may opportunistically exploit nonlinear idiosyncrasies of neural responses to efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information on fast time scales, instead of performing explicit calculation of certain variables.Significance Statement This study aims to understand if linear acceleration information of visual motion is extracted and represented in primate visual motion areas MT and MST. By combining large-scale multi-area neuronal recordings, population-level analyses, and a rich set of moving stimuli, we show that linear acceleration can be decoded from MT activity. Specifically, our results demonstrate that (1) motion acceleration is encoded in MT, and can be directly and quickly decoded from MT ensemble activity, and (2) area MST, despite being a later stage of motion processing, does not refine acceleration representations. These findings call for revisiting how brain areas might efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information from the environment and highlight the importance of temporal dynamics in visual motion processing.

title: Perception of tones versus tone streams under random multi-tone masking and its representation in auditory cortex.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.Significance Statement Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

title: Macaque Area LIP Reflects Confidence-Dependent Changes in Decision Policy.
